hook.line: Tomás keeps getting dates, orders and bills tangled up in the café. Spanish uses the word for knotted string for any time your head, your plans or your paperwork get muddled.
hook.en: I got muddled with so many dates.

examples.en: I got muddled with so many dates.

examples.es: Armaron un enredo con las reservas.
examples.en: They made a mess of the bookings.

examples.es: Tomás se enredó con las cuentas.
examples.en: Tomás got muddled with the accounts.
Did you get muddled with the dates? (informal)

examples.es: Siempre me enredo con los números.
examples.en: I always get muddled with numbers.

rule:
*Enredarse* is to get tangled up, like a cord, and it works for getting muddled. It is reflexive, so *me, te, se, nos* come before the verb: *me enredé con tantas fechas*.

Add *con* (or *en*) and what muddled you.

The noun is *un enredo*, a mess or a mix-up: *¡qué enredo!*, *armaron un enredo*.

English just says "I got muddled". Spanish says "I tangled myself".

*Un lío* is still fine everywhere.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a reflexive verb used figuratively. In Spain people say *liarse*; *enredarse* is the Latin American choice.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick the right form and type the whole sentence: *Tomás ___ con las cuentas.* (se enredó or enredó)
yourTurn.answer: Tomás se enredó con las cuentas.
yourTurn.why: Getting muddled yourself needs *se*, because the verb is reflexive.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I got muddled with so many dates.
yourTurn.why: *Me* goes before *enredé* because it is about yourself.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: What a mess!
yourTurn.why: *Enredo* is the noun for a mess or a mix-up.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: They made a mess of the bookings.
yourTurn.answer: Armaron un enredo con las reservas.
yourTurn.why: *Armar un enredo* is to make a mess, and *con* says of what.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: Did you get muddled with the dates?
Make it about *we*: *Me enredé con el horario.* Say: We got muddled with the schedule.
yourTurn.why: *Nos* goes with *we*, and the verb ends in *-amos*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Me enredé con las fechas.* Say: I did not get muddled with the dates.
yourTurn.answer: No me enredé con las fechas.

pitfalls.wrong: Hay un enredado con el pedido.
pitfalls.right: Hay un enredo con el pedido.
pitfalls.why: Almost. The noun for a mess is *enredo*.

personal: Tell us when you last got muddled, with dates, numbers or directions, using *me enredé con…*.
